Independent Polity
in-duh-PEN-duhnt PAH-lih-tee
n. (a form of church government; congregationalism)
From independent, Latin in- (not) and dependere (to hang from), and polity, Greek politeia, the governance of a body. The term names congregational independency, in which each local church governs itself under Christ.

Biblical Definition

Independent polity, also called congregational independency, is the conviction that each local church is a complete and self-governing body under the sole headship of Christ and the authority of Scripture, answerable to no higher ecclesiastical court or earthly ruler. It holds that Christ has given to every rightly gathered congregation all the officers, ordinances, and authority needful for her own worship, discipline, and government, so that no bishop, synod, or pope stands over her with binding jurisdiction. This does not make the church a lawless democracy nor cut her off from her sisters; rather, she is ruled by her own elders under Christ, and she walks in voluntary fellowship and counsel with other true churches without surrendering her self-government. The 1689 Confession embraces this independency: it confesses that the Lord Jesus, as King and Head of the Church, has appointed a government in the hand of church officers distinct from the civil magistrate, and that each particular congregation is competent under Christ to choose her officers and exercise discipline. Against the prelacy that subjects churches to a chain of bishops, and supremely against the papal monarchy that claims one man as universal head, independent polity insists that Christ alone is Head and that His Word, not the decrees of men, binds the conscience. It honors the dignity Christ has given the local church, refuses the inventions of human hierarchy, and keeps every congregation directly accountable to her one Lord. Thus the autonomy of the local church is no proud isolation but a glad submission to Christ above every earthly authority.

Webster 1828 Definition

Congregational independency: the self-government of each local church under Christ and Scripture, against prelacy and the papal monarchy.

INDEPENDENT POLITY, n. From independent, Latin dependere, to hang from, with in-, not; and polity, Greek politeia, governance.

The principle that each local church is a complete, self-governing body under Christ alone.

Holding that no bishop, synod, or pope bears binding jurisdiction over the local congregation.

Practiced with voluntary fellowship and counsel among true churches, without surrender of self-government.

Founded on Christ’s sole headship: “And gave him to be the head over all things to the church” (Ephesians 1:22).

Key Scripture

Eph 1:22 — "And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church,"

Matt 18:17 — "And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican."

Col 1:18 — "And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence."

Acts 6:3 — "Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business."

Modern Corruption

Independency stands against the prelacy and papal monarchy that subject churches to human hierarchy, and is itself corrupted when autonomy decays into proud isolation or lawlessness.

expand to see more

The corruption independency chiefly opposes is prelacy and, supremely, the papal monarchy, which place over the local church a chain of bishops and at last one man claiming to be universal head and vicar of Christ on earth. But Scripture gives that headship to Christ alone, who is the head of the body, the church, that in all things He might have the preeminence (Colossians 1:18). To erect a human monarch over Christ’s churches is to usurp His throne and to bind the conscience with jurisdiction He never granted. Independency answers that He has equipped each congregation under Himself, so that final discipline rests with the church and her Lord (Matthew 18:17), not with a distant prelate.

Independency has its own besetting corruption when self-government decays into proud isolation, lawlessness, or contempt for the counsel of sister churches. True independency is no autonomy from Christ but submission to Him above every earthly power; the same congregation that bows to no pope must bow wholly to her King and walk in love and accountability with other true churches. To recover the doctrine rightly is to prize the local church’s dignity under Christ while refusing both the tyranny of human hierarchy and the disorder of an independence that answers to no one, not even to the Word.

Hebrew Roots

Independent polity roots in Christ’s sole headship and the competence He gives each local church under His Word.

expand to see more

Each local church is a complete, self-governing body under Christ.

No bishop, synod, or pope holds binding jurisdiction over her.

Final discipline rests with the congregation and her Lord.

Churches walk in voluntary fellowship and counsel without surrendering autonomy.

The 1689 Confession sets forth this congregational independency.

Usage

"“Independent polity confesses no head over the local church but Christ.”"

"“The Baptists held an independency that rejected prelacy and the papal claim alike.”"

"“True independency is submission to Christ, not isolation from His people.”"
